findings.description: The instance user_data script exports a static AWS access key ID and secret access key in cleartext. EC2 user data is retrievable from the instance metadata service by any process or SSRF-capable application on the host, and the secret is stored unencrypted in the launch configuration and in version control.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the instance's root EBS volume is created without encryption at rest, leaving data on disk and in derived snapshots unprotected.

No metadata_options block requiring http_tokens = "required" is set, so the instance permits IMDSv1. Combined with the credentials placed in user data, an SSRF flaw in the Apache workload could retrieve them directly from the metadata endpoint.

The instance is launched into aws_subnet.web_subnet, which is associated with a route table routing 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway, and its public DNS is exported as an output; combined with the web-node security group it places the host directly on the internet.
The EBS volume is created without encrypted = true (the attribute is explicitly commented out), so data written to the volume and any snapshots taken from it are stored unencrypted.

The EBS snapshot is created without encryption (no encrypted/KMS key configuration, and the source volume is not confirmed encrypted), so block-level data including any sensitive content is stored unencrypted and can be restored by anyone with snapshot access.
Ingress rule allows TCP port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH administration on the attached instance/ENI to the entire internet and enabling brute-force and exploitation attempts.
Port 80 is open to 0.0.0.0/0 with no corresponding TLS (443) listener, so traffic to the web host is transmitted in cleartext over the public internet.
Egress permits all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, providing no outbound network segmentation and facilitating data exfiltration or command-and-control traffic from a compromised host.

The subnet sets map_public_ip_on_launch = true, so every instance launched into it (including aws_instance.web_host) automatically receives a public IPv4 address and becomes reachable from the internet, expanding attack surface and bypassing network segmentation.

The subnet sets map_public_ip_on_launch = true, automatically exposing any launched instance directly to the internet rather than requiring explicit, deliberate public IP assignment behind a NAT or load balancer.

The VPC does not manage/restrict its default security group (no aws_default_security_group resource), leaving the AWS default group that permits all intra-group traffic available for accidental attachment to workloads.

A default route 0.0.0.0/0 is pointed at the internet gateway on the route table associated with both subnets, making them public subnets. Combined with instances/ENIs placed in these subnets, this removes any network segmentation boundary and exposes workloads directly to the internet.

The second subnet is associated with the same route table that carries a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway, so no private subnet tier exists in this VPC; every workload placed in either subnet is internet-routable.

The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (no aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration or sse block), so sensitive network telemetry is stored unencrypted by configuration intent.
No public access block or ACL/bucket policy restrictions are defined for the flow log bucket, leaving it reliant on account defaults to avoid public exposure of network log data.
The bucket has no server access logging configured, so unauthorized access to stored VPC flow logs would leave no audit trail.
Versioning is not enabled and force_destroy = true is set, so log objects (and the whole bucket) can be irrecoverably deleted or overwritten by an attacker seeking to destroy evidence.
No bucket policy enforcing aws:SecureTransport is attached, so flow log data may be read or written over unencrypted HTTP connections.
